newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says committed to Alpha space station.
newsitem.headline: Russia says committed to Alpha space station.

text.p: Russian space officials said on Wednesday they were committed to the international Alpha space station and would use a new government loan to fund the Russian modules of the craft.
Boris Ostroumov, deputy head of the Russian Space Agency, told Reuters the 800 billion rouble ($140 million) loan could be paid by the end of this month.
"We plan to spend all the sum to finance the Alpha project," he said. "Russia does not plan to drop out of the project."
Russia is building the two important modules of the space station, an international project which will replace the ageing Mir orbiting station.
The first module, a storage centre, is due to be launched in June next year, followed by the service module, where the cosmonauts will live and work.
"We hope that the service module of the Alpha will be ready to be launched in December 1998," Ostroumov said.
Russia's ability to meet its promises on the space station has been in doubt since February, when Moscow said it would have to postpone the launch of the first module.
Alpha is to be assembled in stages by 2003, and so a delay to one section could put the entire project at risk and some Western officials said Russia should be forced out of the plan.
The United States, the European Space Agency, Canada, Italy and Japan are partners in the project.

Russian space agency head Yury Koptev said last week that the Moscow government had promised to lend the space sector a total of 1.5 trillion roubles ($261 million) in April and May to fund the service module.
The space sector was one of the most proud and cosseted industries in Soviet days, but it has faced problems since the superpower fell apart and funding became much tighter.
Koptev said last week that, if the government paid the promised $261 million, Russia would meet its obligations.

The U.S. space agency NASA said it wanted to take $200 million from its Space Shuttle budget to pay for contingency plans if the Russians do not deliver on time, and an additional $100 million to help the Russian programme.
